title: Matplotlib Examples
description: Small Matplotlib examples from the lessons. Each example links back to its explanation and practice task.

examples.title: Figures and axes
examples.description: A figure is the whole chart image. An Axes object is an area inside it where data is drawn.
examples.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 3])
plt.show()

examples.title: Label the meaning
examples.description: Axis labels explain what values mean and which units they use. A title tells the reader the chart's topic.
examples.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 3])
ax.set_xlabel("Day")
ax.set_ylabel("Books read")
ax.set_title("Reading this week")
plt.show()

examples.title: Compare categories with bars
examples.description: A bar chart compares categories. Bars usually start from zero so their lengths fairly represent the values.
examples.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(["Art", "Music", "Sport"], [3, 5, 4])
ax.set_ylabel("Votes")
plt.show()

examples.title: Use a scatter plot for pairs
examples.description: A scatter plot shows paired measurements as separate points. It helps reveal a relationship without connecting every point.
examples.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter([1, 2, 3], [4, 3, 5])
ax.set_xlabel("Practice sessions")
ax.set_ylabel("Points")
plt.show()

examples.title: Histograms group numeric values
examples.description: A histogram groups numbers into bins and counts how many fall in each bin. A bin is an interval, not a category label.
examples.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist([1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3], bins=[0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5])
ax.set_xlabel("Books per learner")
ax.set_ylabel("Learners")
plt.show()

examples.title: Legends identify series
examples.description: A legend matches a line or marker to its label. It is useful when one chart has more than one series.
examples.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2], [2, 3], label="Red team")
ax.plot([1, 2], [3, 4], label="Blue team")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

examples.title: Control visible limits carefully
examples.description: Axis limits choose the part of the number range shown. Use them deliberately and tell readers when a narrow range matters.
examples.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [8, 9, 10])
ax.set_ylim(0, 12)
plt.show()

examples.title: Place two plots in one figure
examples.description: subplots can create several plotting areas. Give each area clear labels so readers can compare them correctly.
examples.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
axes[0].bar(["A", "B"], [2, 3])
axes[1].plot([1, 2], [3, 4])
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

examples.title: Grid lines support reading
examples.description: A light grid can help readers estimate values. It should support the data rather than overpower it.
examples.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 3])
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

examples.title: Save a figure to a file
examples.description: savefig writes the figure to a file. Choose a format and size appropriate for how it will be used.
examples.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(["Books", "Pens"], [2, 3])
fig.savefig("practice-chart.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

examples.title: Explain missing observations
examples.description: Missing data should not be silently shown as a real zero. A gap can honestly show that no observation was recorded.
examples.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [2, float("nan"), 4], marker="o")
plt.show()

examples.title: Review the story the chart tells
examples.description: A chart should answer a clear question without exaggerating. Check title, units, scale and the underlying values before sharing.
examples.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(["Monday", "Tuesday"], [4, 5])
ax.set_ylabel("Books borrowed")
ax.set_title("Fictional library example")
ax.set_ylim(0, 6)
plt.show()
